title: Who is the Jack in a deck of cards? | GAME WORDS

entries.note: Old English, with Germanic cognates meaning joy or fun; once meant general fun, games, hunting for sport, and was long a euphemism for sex.
An old euphemism for a sex worker, from the use of [[from:game]] as a euphemism for sex.
A phrase still sometimes heard, though less and less, left over from [[from:game]] as a euphemism for sex.
Also to have game: an old phrase meaning to have the mettle or fighting spirit for a contest, apparently comparing someone to a [[see:gamecock]].
A fighting rooster, apparently the comparison behind [[see:to be game]].
Related to [[from:game]], with the frequentative [[see:-le]] ending, so it means being at the activity of gaming; apparently not related to [[unrelated:gambol]].
Jess wondered if it was related to [[unrelated:gamble]], but it comes from a word for a horse's leg and meant skipping or leaping.
A frequentative ending, as in Old English, marking a repeated activity, as in [[see:gamble]] and [[see:chuckle]], and perhaps in [[see:Wordle]].
Via French [[from:poquer]] from German [[from:pochen]], which now means to knock but used to mean to brag, which suits the bluffing; an older version was [[see:brag]].
An old version of [[see:poker]] popular in Britain; its name matches the older meaning of [[see:pochen]].
The one-player card game, from the French word for solitary; it was also a word for a widow or a recluse.
A card game like [[see:blackjack]] whose name is a bad anglicisation of French [[from:vingt-et-un]], twenty-one; it has nothing to do with floating pontoons.
An American name from 19th-century casinos that paid extra for an ace of spades with a black jack; it replaced [[see:twenty-one]].
The English version of French [[from:vingt-et-un]], the game's name before [[see:blackjack]] replaced it.
From French [[from:binocle]], eyeglasses, after the paired card combinations in the game; it also had odd variants like peek knuckle.
Thought to be another garbled foreign name, from Russian [[from:biritch]].
Also called Russian whist, the game behind [[gave:bridge]]; it may come from a Russian word for herald or from Ottoman Turkish [[from?:bir üç]], one three.
Of uncertain origin: one theory links it to [[from?:whiskey poker]], another to German card terms meaning glory or fame.
A game in which an extra hand is dealt that the first player to discard may take; one theory says it gave us [[gave?:rummy]].
A Spanish game based on [[from:rummy]], whose English name is a bad attempt at Spanish [[from:con quién]], with whom.
A 1680 quote says the game is named for the silence kept during play, from an old word whist, be quiet, which fed into [[gave:wistfulness]].
Appears to blend the old word [[from:whist]], be quiet, with [[from:wishfulness]], making it more pensive than plain silence.
From Old French [[from:esches]], chessmen, plural of [[from:eschec]], the game's name, ultimately from Persian [[from:shah]], king; originally called [[see:chaturanga]] in Sanskrit.
Every sense, including ticking a box and the bank slip, comes from chess via Old French [[from:eschec]]; the money senses come through [[see:exchequer]].
Means killer, likely from Latin [[from:mactare]], to kill, but possibly related to Arabic [[from?:mata]], he died, as in [[see:shah mat]].
An English folk-etymology rendering of [[from:shah mat]].
In Persian it meant the king is astonished or left helpless; in Arabic mat was read as he died; source of [[gave:checkmate]].
The French [[equivalent:checkmate]], the closest Romance version of [[from:shah mat]]; its mat is the same one found in [[same-root:matador]].
The original Sanskrit name of [[see:chess]].
From Old French [[from:eschec]]; originally a chessboard, then linked with accounting because Norman England did its sums on a cloth divided into squares.
The UK finance minister's title, which keeps the word [[see:exchequer]] alive.
Jess says it comes from a French word for a pledge or security, perhaps because pawns are a line of defence; same root as German [[same-root:Pfand]].
The German deposit paid on drink bottles and refunded when they are returned; same root as [[same-root:pawn]] and Scandinavian [[same-root:pant]].
The deposit on Scandinavian beer cans, from the same source as [[same-root:Pfand]].
From Sanskrit [[from:ratha]], chariot, because an Indian form of chess used chariots instead of castles; not from a [[unrelated:crow's nest]], as Jess guessed.
The German name for the chess knight, after the way the piece jumps.
A Spanish name for the chess queen.
The Spanish name for the chess knight, which means horse rather than [[see:caballero]], since the piece only shows a horse.
What you might expect the Spanish knight to be called, instead of [[see:caballo]].
The US name for [[see:draughts]], named after the board, which makes sense given that [[see:exchequer]] once meant a chessboard.
The British name for [[see:checkers]], from the verb [[from:draw]], to move, after the pieces being moved around the board.
A blend of clue and [[from:Ludo]], patented in the 1940s by a British musician inspired by murder mysteries and the parlour game [[see:Murder (game)]].
The US name for [[see:Cluedo]], perhaps changed because Americans don't know [[see:Ludo]]; also a film Jess calls one of her favourite comedies.
Latin for I play; a board game originally called [[from:pachisi]], whose name forms part of [[see:Cluedo]].
A parlour game played to pass the evenings, which inspired the inventor of [[see:Cluedo]].
Her novels, published from the 1920s, made mysteries popular and inspired games like [[see:Cluedo]].
A [[see:Cluedo]] character who was originally Nurse White.
A [[see:Cluedo]] character originally called Colonel Yellow; Rob thinks Colonel Mustard is a much better name.
An Americanised adaptation of the Indian game [[from:pachisi]]; Jess says its board layout looks similar to [[see:Clue]]'s.
An Indian cross-and-circle board game named after twenty-five, the highest throw of the dice; it was the original of [[gave:Ludo]].
Rob's childhood version of [[see:Ludo]] with a popping die dome, named for the frustration of being sent back to the start; called [[see:Trouble]] in the US.
Pointed out in passing as the correct singular of dice.
The US name for [[see:Frustration]], which had a cute advertising jingle in the 1990s.
From roots meaning one and many, after one person owning as much as possible; the game was copied by [[see:Charles Darrow]] from [[from:The Landlord's Game]].
In the 1500s, something made exclusively by one vineyard, like a specific champagne; also an unrelated physics term for a single pole.
Game designer, writer and feminist who created [[see:The Landlord's Game]], sold her patent for $500 and got no credit until after her death.
Reformer whose anti-monopoly single tax theory [[see:The Landlord's Game]] was designed to illustrate.
[[see:Lizzie Magie]]'s educational game showing the harms of monopolising land, playable as [[see:Prosperity]] or [[see:Monopolist]]; its board looks just like [[see:Monopoly]]'s.
The anti-monopolist way to play [[see:The Landlord's Game]], in which everyone is rewarded when wealth is created.
The way to play [[see:The Landlord's Game]] by creating monopolies and crushing opponents.
Played [[see:The Landlord's Game]] at a dinner party, asked for the rules, then sold it as [[see:Monopoly]], claiming he invented it in his basement.
Bought the rights to [[see:Monopoly]] from [[see:Charles Darrow]], then paid [[see:Lizzie Magie]] $500 for her patent.
Invented by [[see:Leslie Scott]], who named it after Swahili [[from:kujenga]], to build.
British inventor of [[see:Jenga]], born in Africa and fluent in Swahili.
Named because you send your opponent's pieces back to the start; nothing to do with [[unrelated:gammon]]; a very old game once called [[see:tabula]].
What [[see:backgammon]] was called in Mesopotamia, where the game is said to be about 5,000 years old.
Named after scrabbling around for words or tiles; invented in 1938 by [[see:Alfred Mosher Butts]], who based tile values on letter frequency and first called it [[see:Lexiko]].
Its inventor counted letters in a pile of documents, much as [[see:Alfred Mosher Butts]] later did for [[see:Scrabble]].
Invented [[see:Scrabble]] in 1938, reportedly setting letter values by counting the letters on a New York Times front page.
The original name of [[see:Scrabble]], which Jess likes a lot.
Along with [[see:za]], a short word that players complain has ruined [[see:Scrabble]] now that everyone knows it.
Along with [[see:xi]], a short word that players complain has ruined [[see:Scrabble]] now that everyone knows it.
The highest-scoring single [[see:Scrabble]] play under North American rules, earning [[see:Michael Cresta]] 365 points.
The plural of a bird name, valid under international [[see:Scrabble]] rules; it earned [[see:Karl Khoshnaw]] 392 points.
Played across all three triple word scores and crossing words like opacifying, it would score a hypothetical 1,780 points in [[see:Scrabble]].
Rob starts with [[see:stare]], experts suggest [[see:tales]] or [[see:slates]], and Jess notes the name's [[see:-le]] ending, which suggests something done repeatedly.
Rob's usual [[see:Wordle]] starter, with the common consonants R, T and S and the vowels A and E.
The Science Foundation of Ireland's best [[see:Wordle]] starter, though Wordle rarely uses plurals.
The best [[see:Wordle]] starter according to WordleBot; an anagram of [[see:tales]].
With [[see:trial]], the two-seed [[see:Wordle]] opening recommended by the Science Foundation of Ireland to narrow down the answer.
The second word of the two-seed [[see:Wordle]] opening, played after [[see:cones]].
An imitative word, [[from:chuck]], to breathe suddenly and sharply, plus the frequentative [[see:-le]]; blended into [[gave:chortle]].
[[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s blend of [[from:chuckle]] and [[from:snort]], covered in the hosts' portmanteau episode.
The dance game invented in Tobago; probably a Creole form of [[from?:limber]] rather than, as a less likely theory says, the border of hell.
A bean bag toss named because the bags were full of corn; originally called [[see:parlor quoits]].
The original name of [[see:cornhole]].
Not an acronym for [[see:touch and go]], since the name is older; just a word for tapping someone, with variants like tig and [[see:tick]].
Rob's school name for [[see:tag (game)]]; the hosts say tick or tech goes back to Middle English.
Rob's version of [[see:tick]], where caught players were stuck standing in a chalk circle, the glue pot, until someone freed them.
Simon is apparently [[see:Simon Peter]], a follower who did what Jesus said, though the name may predate this church-approved reading.
The British name for [[equivalent:Simon says]]; Rob advises against obeying anyone called Simple Simon.
Said to be the Simon of [[see:Simon says]], as a disciple who mostly did what Jesus said.
The card was originally the [[see:knave]], renamed because K stood for king; Jack is a generic everyman name, as in [[see:jack-o'-lantern]].
Discussed in the hosts' Halloween episode, along with Jack as a generic name.
The original name of the [[see:jack]] card, changed because K already stood for king.
The French [[equivalent:Simon says]], also the title of a song.
Another French version of [[equivalent:Simon says]].
The Afrikaans [[equivalent:Simon says]].
The Arabic [[equivalent:Simon says]], as the hosts translate it.
The Basque [[equivalent:Simon says]].
The Bengali [[equivalent:Simon says]], which the hosts render as leader or teacher says.
The Japanese [[equivalent:Simon says]], in which a ship's captain gives the orders.
Apparently a Spanish [[equivalent:Simon says]], though the hosts aren't sure how widely it is used.
Originally a riddle; the hosts plan to cover it in a future episode on riddles and puzzles.
